title: Questions, question tags, indirect questions
subtitle: Question forms, tags, and polite indirect questions

rows.statement: **Am / Was** I on time? · **Are / Were** you tired? · **Is / Was** he cold?
rows.question: be + subject + …

rows.statement: **Am / Was** I interrupting you? · **Are / Were** you going on a picnic?
rows.question: be + subject + -ing

rows.statement: **Have / Had** you got any money? · **Has / Had** she finished?
rows.question: have + subject + past participle

rows.person: have as a main verb, and other verbs
rows.statement: **Do / Did** they have enough time? · **Does / Did** he need anything?
rows.question: do / does / did + subject + infinitive

rows.statement: **Should** I wait? · **Could** you help me? · **Will** she be here soon?
rows.negative: Invert the modal and the subject.
rows.question: modal + subject + infinitive

rows.person: who, whose, whom, what, which, where, when, why, how
rows.statement: **Who** is taking the rubbish out? · **What** is the weather like? · **Where** did you go?
rows.negative: Question word first, then normal question order.
rows.question: question word + auxiliary + subject

blocks.text: With the question words **who** and **what**, whether we use **do** or not depends on whether the question word refers to the subject or object of the verb.
blocks.note: Subject: **Who saw you?** (= Someone saw you. Who?) · Object: **Who did you see?** (= You saw someone. Who?)

blocks.correct: **Did you go** to the talk on the environment?
blocks.incorrect: **Did you went** to the talk on the environment?

items: Remember that after **do / does**, we use the bare infinitive. **Does Tom want** a glass of orange juice? (not *Does Tom wants*)
Remember that the verb **mean** forms questions just like other main verbs. **What does 'environmental' mean?** (not *What means 'environmental'?*)

rows.question: You are Canadian, **aren't you**? · She is beautiful, **isn't she**?
We **are having** the lesson early tomorrow, **aren't we**? · People **should** recycle things, **shouldn't they**? · There **will be** lots of people there, **won't there**?
Tom has a lovely voice, **hasn't / doesn't he**?
Frank lives in Germany now, **doesn't he**? · Your friends really enjoyed themselves at the party, **didn't they**?
Let's get a DVD tonight, **shall we**?
Pass me that book, **will / would / could you**? · Don't forget tonight, **will you**?

rows.use: To ask someone to agree with us (falling intonation)
To check whether something is true (rising intonation)

blocks.text: In sentences with **I am**, we use **aren't I?** as the question tag. In sentences with **I am not**, we use **am I?**
blocks.note: I'm the best student in the class, **aren't I**? · I'm not very tall, **am I**?

items: With **everyone, no one** and **someone**, we use question tags with a plural verb and **they**. Everyone's going to be there, **aren't they**? · No one wants to come, **do they**? · Someone's been in here, **haven't they**?

Usually, when we have a positive verb in a sentence, we use a negative question tag. When we have a negative verb in a sentence, we use a positive question tag. With a negative word like **no, little, never, nobody, no one, hardly**, etc., we use a positive question tag. You **have got** no manners, **have you**? · We **never** enjoy our holiday, **do we**?
In sentences where the subject is **there**, we repeat **there** in the question tag. There's no point calling Tim now, **is there**?

blocks.text: In American English, a question tag with **do** can be used after a sentence with **have got**. This is not usually done in British English.
blocks.note: US: They've got a lot of money, **don't they**? · UK: They've got a lot of money, **haven't they**?

blocks.text: Form: introductory phrase or question + clause with normal word order. We use indirect questions when we want to ask questions politely.

rows.example: **Could you tell me** what time it is?
**Could you let me know** when it starts?
**Do you know** who that woman is?

rows.use: I wonder if you could tell me …
rows.example: **I wonder if you could tell me** how much this costs.
**I wonder if you know** what the starting salary is.
**I would like to know** what your company is going to do about it.

blocks.text: We do not use question word order in the second part of the sentence.
blocks.note: I would like to know when **the next train to London leaves**. (not *when does the next train to London leave*)

items: Some indirect questions, which begin with a question word, need a question mark at the end. **Could you tell me where the library is?**
If a direct question is a yes/no question, the equivalent indirect question uses **if** or **whether**. I wonder **if / whether** you have read this book.

exercises.title: C · Help us help the environment
exercises.instruction: Complete using the words in the box. Use each word only once. There is one extra word you do not need to use.

items.prompt: (1) ___ responsibility is it to look after the environment? Yours!
And (2) ___ should you start? Right now is the answer!
But (3) ___ is going to help you? We are! We are GreenWarriors,
(4) ___ me? We all have a responsibility to the world around us.
But (5) ___ can I make a difference? By recycling your paper, glass and plastic
(6) ___ 's the first step? The first step is to come along to the GreenWarrior offices
(7) ___ other organisations are you connected to? GreenWarriors is a completely independent protest organisation.
(8) ___ is GreenWarriors based? We are a national organisation, with our headquarters in Northampton.

exercises.title: E · Early humans and the weather
exercises.instruction: Write one word in each gap.

items.prompt: (1) ___ you think you understand the weather?
For early humans, the weather was a constant source of questions. (2) ___ is it raining?
What (3) ___ this storm mean?
Where (4) ___ the wind go when it blows?
People came up with many explanations for the weather, usually involving gods or ancestors. (5) ___ you explain what a rainbow is?
The weather has also been used to explain other things. What would you say if someone asked you (6) ___ kangaroos come from?
You'd probably say Australia, but (7) ___ did the Aborigines explain these strange animals?
Finally, the wind died down and the kangaroos landed on the ground. (8) ___ could they be?
